reviews.title: It works fine, but...
reviews.body: I was really excited for this USB hub, but it has way less utility for me than I realized. I typically work off of a docking station and switch between my personal and work MacBooks on it. The docking station is a pretty old one and it doesn't have any USB-C ports, so I can't plug this into it directly with the included cable. At first I figured, no problem, I'll just grab a C to A cable and plug it in with that. I was about to, and was assessing which of my old, janky USB hubs could have their connected accessories moved over to this much sleeker hub, when I realized that my worst USB hub has 7 ports, all in use, and they are all USB-A. So I could move over 4/7 accessories to this hub, but would either need to use A to C converters for the rest of them or keep using the old, unreliable hub anyway for three of the things (or plug the old hub into this one and have 3 accessories connected to this new hub while 4 remained plugged into the old one which is going through a second layer of hub-ness now). I should have thought this through before ordering, but I have exactly zero peripherals that connect to my computer with a USB-C plug. I know that is slowly changing over time, but it makes sense because so many older computers (and docking stations) don't have any USB-C ports. My personal MacBook Pro M3 does, and I could connect this hub directly to my MacBook with the included USB-C to C cable, but there would be no point to because I don't have any accessories that use a USB-C connection. I have a TON of peripherals, including the basics like a keyboard, mouse, and webcam, as well as some less common things like a Wacom tablet I don't use very often, but literally none of them come with a C to C cable, even if they have a C connection on the peripheral itself, as is the case with my current daily driver keyboard. I could swap out the cable for a C to C one so that I could use this dock, but that feels like more trouble than it's worth. I did set it up to test the charging capabilities, and it does give 45W according to the System Report on my MacBook Pro M3. Usually it takes about 65W to keep it charged while actively in use, but 45W is fine for overnight charging or light use, in my experience. All that being said, I just don't really have much use for this, although it does appear to be as advertised. Not knocking any stars because it does work as expected, it's just not useful to me, personally.

reviews.title: Excellent powered USB Hub
reviews.body: This is a well-made powered hub. Delivery was same day (awesome) and arrived undamaged due to excellent packaging. Upon testing, all of my ports worked with no problem. I like the slanted design, which makes it easy to plug and unplug your USB cables. There are plenty of ports, including 6-USB and 3-USB C ports. All USB ports can charge as well as be used for data. 3 of the USB ports move data at 5 GBS and 2 of the USB ports move data at 10 GBS. 2 of the USB-C ports are for charging only and 1-USB C port is for charging and data. I plugged in a USB portable thumb drive, and it was recognized immediately with no issue. I am not running any other disks off of this hub at this time. Not only that, but I was pleasantly surprised by post sales support. I had a question on submitting my warranty registration using their website. They only design issue I have is that the power plug and USB C connection cable comes out the side of the unit. reviews.title: Provides the power requirements of your USB devices while extending the available ports.
reviews.body: I had a problem. My monitor array at home includes a Thunderbolt hub that includes two DisplayPort and one VGA connector, and my laptop at home includes one HDMI and one additional VGA connector, but this totals only 6 screens when my laptop's primary screen is added in. My monitor array, on the other hand, includes yet another 6 screens (all but two of them are 1080p). These screens are driven by a set of mostly DisplayLink display adapters, although I have a few others that required manually installed drivers (with varying success), and some that don't advertise DisplayLink but whose drivers installed automatically anyways. Six USB-A Display adapters require a lot of power, and I ran into the limit of my workstation and Thunderbolt hub's power capacity at only 4 additional displays, and every single USB-A and USB-C port on my laptop and my dock were used up, leading to a messy snarl of wires and cables that wire ties just didn't resolve. What I like: 1. It allows me to connect my entire array of video extenders and power my entire array of monitors. It substantially cleans up the mess of cables connected to my laptop and hub by putting many of them in one place. 2. Its aluminum finish looks good on my desktop. 3. Its power supply is rated for 65w, telling me I can connect more devices before its capacity is exhausted. 4. It has a sturdy construction. What I don't like: a. Ummm, that's a tough one. Maybe it takes up additional desk space and there are a lot of cables connected to it, but hey, that's kind-of the intent. Nah, I can't say I dislike that. Caveats: - Your results may vary if you plan to use this to drive a large array of screens. My laptop has 64GB RAM and a second video card with another 6GB video RAM. I have a newer laptop at work with 128GB RAM and a second video card with 16GB video RAM that can't run my home array without overheating.

So far, it's performing well, has given me more charging capacity, and I still have space left for additional devices if I decide to add more. Overall, it was worth the cost of this particular item.

reviews.title: Performed well until it didn't, but replaced promptly without hassle.
reviews.body: This USB hub worked well for 9 months then it started intermittently not communicating, then it would reconnect. All I had connected at those disconnect times were Logitech dongles for a keyboard and trackball. Difficult to diagnose, I thought the screen was freezing, perhaps a graphics card issue. Occasionally Windows issued the "USB device not connected." When the hub completely failed, the diagnosis was easy. I contacted intpw via email as suggested on their website, after a couple of efforts at diagnosis they agreed the unit was defective and replaced it promptly through Amazon. The service tech suggested that Logitech dongles should be placed as far apart at possible on the hub, they are known to interfere with each other if too close; don't know that I've ever had that problem, but took the advice. So yeah, it would have been nice if it didn't fail, but stuff happens and they replaced it. This thing is really well made, an aluminum extrusion with the board rigidly mounted inside, shielded and physically protected.

reviews.title: Low profile, fast, and stylish
reviews.body: There is not much to say about this. It has a low profile and lets you expand how many USB ports you have. The first four USB A ports, starting from the left, have 5Gb/s speeds. The next two have 10Gb/s speeds. What you should know is that of the three USB C ports on the right, the first one has 10Gb/s speeds, the next two are just for power and do not handle data. If you have a phone or tablet that lets you charge it through a USB C port, you can plug it into one of those ports and it will charge. What you should know is that you need to plug this into a high-speed USB 3.2 port to get the fast speeds. It comes with a USB C to USB C data cable for plugging into your computer. Since it only gives you one USB C data port, you're not gaining any additional USB C ports since you use one from your computer and only get one in return. The cable isn't that long, so you'll be limited in where you can place it unless you invest in a longer cable. But the price is good, it looks nice, and is very functional.

reviews.title: Solidly built powered USB hub (with a few wrinkles)
reviews.body: This hub has a very Apple-esque design and appears to be very solidly built. So far, it seems to perform well and as expected based on its specs. A couple of things though that are not made clear to purchasers based on the description provided: 1. The hub is provided only with a US 2-pin mains power lead. In other countries you’ll need to use a plug adaptor, else provide your own native mains cord with an IEC-C7 “figure 8” connector on the other end. At least the power brick uses that style of connector, the mains plug is not hard-wired. 2. The instructions warn you that WiFi dongles (such as those used to communicate with wireless mouse and keyboards) should not be plugged into the hub due to the risk of interference. Meaning one port on your laptop/PC will have to be used for such dongles if you have them. Not a dealbreaker, but it would have been nice to know this prior. 3. The instructions say only one HDD or two SSDs can be connected to the hub (presumably for power draw reasons). The maximum load is 900 mA (4.5 W) but it’s not clear if that is per data port (the USB standard) or in total across all data ports. This hub provides only one USB-C and two USB-A 3.1 Gen 2 data ports (10 Gbps). That’s a bit light-on these days. The remainder are USB-A 3.0 ports (5 Gbps). The two “power delivery” (non-data) USB-C ports are handy for charging devices, total power delivery max 45 W. So all up, a rating of 4 stars.

Pros Great selection of ports without being excessive Reliable performance Compact but well built Premium-feeling materials Works well for both travel and desktop setups Cons Requires an adequately powered USB-C charger for the best experience Port selection may not fit every specialized setup Final Thoughts This has been a great USB-C hub. reviews.title: I don't know how I ever lived without it.
reviews.body: I'm very happy with this device. My laptop doesn't have an ethernet port and only has one USB-C SuperSpeed port, so I bought an ethernet to USB-C cable to connect my ethernet switch to the Anker and into my laptop's USB-C port, and it works great. I don't need a fast internet connection for the things I do, so my service is only a 50mbps symmetrical up/down connection, and that's what I get even while transferring files from my external between other devices, charging my phone, and using composite devices. I bought the Anker 100W Compact and Foldable USB C Charger for it and it charges my S24 extremely fast. It's very well built, yet super lightweight. I love the sleek, slender design. It's the perfect size to easily slide into a pocket, store in a desk drawer, or keep handy in a laptop case or backpack. Using it is easy. Just plug it into your computer and plug your devices into it. Just make sure you have a power supply for it if you're charging or powering other devices, using external storage, or running anything else that taxes USB power. I have had ZERO connectivity issues with it — no random disconnect/reconnect blips, no failed transfers for huge amounts of data that have taken up to 45 minutes, no static his or crackle when my headset is running through it... no problems at all. It's actually kind of spooky now that I think about it... I can't recall a time I've ever had a similar device that didn't have some nuance that got under my skin, like a loose connection, random disconnections, having to reinstall the drivers all the time, or having to troubleshoot just to get it connected for the first time. The most stress I've put it through was with my keyboard connected, ethernet running through it, my S24 charging and transferring about ~20gb of pictures and videos to my 2T external HD at the same time that my laptop was transferring about ~500gb of media and documents to the HD, too, and I was surprised by how warm it DIDN'T get. My only complaint is trivial and unique to my situation — I wish output cord was longer. About six inches would do. My laptop sits up on an adjustable stand that clamps to my desk, and the end where the output cord is hangs a few inches off of my desk. This puts extra stress on the USB-C port and can wear it out faster or damage it. I haven't had a use for the HDMI port yet, but I eventually will. I use all of the other ports for my work and personal devices, though. These include: a 2tb external hard drive; a Poly Blackwire 3320 Series headset; a dongle for a wireless mouse/keyboard combo or a wired keyboard and a dongle for a wireless mouse; my Galaxy S24 charges and transfers files through it super fast; I have several thumb drives ranging from 20gb to 512gb that I regularly use; I recently bought an RCA/S Video-to-USB converter to digitize old home movies I plug into it, too.

reviews.title: A sleek, full-size hub that finally got everything right for my laptop setup
reviews.body: I recently picked up the Anker USB-C Hub (5-in-1, 4K HDMI + 90W Power Delivery), and it’s quickly become one of the most used accessories in my gear setup. The build is solid—aluminum shell, clean finish, and it matches my laptop’s aesthetic nicely. Plugged it in and it immediately recognized every device: external monitor, USB-A hard drive, flash drive, mouse, and power all at once. No compatibility headaches, which is already a huge win. The performance has been great. The 4K HDMI output works flawlessly with my external monitor, offering crisp picture quality and no weird dropouts or lag. The 90 W Power Delivery means my laptop charges even when I’m using it hard (video editing + screen output + USB devices), which used to be a pain when using lesser hubs that throttle the charging or heat up quickly. The USB-A ports feel robust and haven't failed or lagged with connected accessories, and the entire hub remains cool under load. What really seals the five-star rating for me is the combination of reliability, design, and simplicity. There’s no dongle nonsense, no weird firmware updates needed, just solid performance. It hides neatly behind the laptop and stays connected without getting pulled out accidentally. If you work with laptops, external screens, and multiple devices—and want something streamlined that won’t get in the way—this Anker hub is absolutely worth it.

A few things I really like: * Compact and lightweight but still feels high quality * Clean/simple setup without a million cords * Didn’t overheat * Great for turning a laptop into an actual workstation * Anker quality is usually reliable and this feels no different Honestly one of those purchases that just quietly makes life easier. reviews.title: Misleading Speed Claims — Test Your Ports Before You Trust Them
reviews.body: I did a thorough technical investigation of this hub by analyzing Linux kernel USB enumeration logs, so this review is based on hard data rather than impressions. The good: The hub is solidly built and the included 5V 3A power adapter does improve stability. The two USB-A ports on the ends of the hub (ports 1 and 2 in my testing) delivered genuine SuperSpeed 5 Gbps throughput, and so did the two USB-A ports on the opposite end (ports 7 and 8). So four of the seven ports do actually perform well for fast storage devices. The bad: The title claims "10Gbps" — this is simply false. The hub is built around VIA Labs USB 3.1 Gen 1 silicon, which is a 5 Gbps technology, not 10 Gbps. Not a single port on this hub is capable of 10 Gbps under any circumstances. The ugly: All three USB-C ports — the ones most likely to be used with modern high-speed devices — are wired through a USB 2.0 only signal path internally. Despite the USB-C connector implying modern speeds, these ports max out at 480 Mbps, roughly 1/10th of what the product title advertises. Plugging anything into the USB-C ports also causes the hub's internal Terminus controller to reset and power cycle, briefly disrupting all other connected devices. This happened consistently with and without the power adapter connected. Internal topology for the technically curious: The hub contains three separate hub controllers internally — a Terminus Technology FE1.1 (USB 2.0) at the top level, and two VIA Labs 2824 controllers as sub-hubs. The USB-C ports are routed exclusively through the 2.0-only signal paths of these sub-hubs with no SuperSpeed wiring whatsoever. Bottom line: If you only need the USB-A ports and can live with 5 Gbps instead of the advertised 10 Gbps, it works fine. But if you bought this specifically for fast USB-C connectivity, you will be disappointed. The product title is misleading on both the speed rating and the implied capability of the USB-C ports.

reviews.title: Amazing affordable USB-C Hub, works with M1 Pro 14, Windows 11 Laptop, and Nintendo Switch 1.
reviews.body: Due to just one problem, I would rate this more of a 4.5/5. Very rarely, I'll have issues with power draw, and the hub won't work while connected. However, after just unplugging and plugging things back in, it fixes the problem fast. Of all USB-C hubs I've looked at, this one is probably the most affordable (I bought at 16 USD) and has the best HDMI, USB-A, and USB-C ports for the price. I've used this on my MacBook M1 Pro 14, my Windows 11 laptop, and what surprised me was that it even worked on my Nintendo Switch 1, for display and power. It's very versatile. Ports: With the single HDMI port, I can connect my 1440p monitor at its max refresh rate (144Hz), and I tested my 4K TV (60Hz) all without problems, unlike some USB-C Hubs that can have stuttering. I've tested the USB-A ports with my keyboard and mouse, which work flawlessly. For my main use, I connect a data cable from the USB Hub (connected to any of my devices) to my KVM switch, so if you want to use it for a KVM setup, I highly recommend it. The USB-C ports also worked really well with my external drives. I do some light video editing, but even 4K video on my editing timeline worked amazingly. Build Quality: The shell itself is nothing spectacular; it's good and gets the job done, absolutely no complaints. The cable actually feels way better than the other USB Hubs I've had. It appears to have a braided cable, but all I know is that it isn't rubber, which is what I prefer. Because of that, I feel confident putting it in a bag without worrying about the cable getting squished, bent, or damaged (though I don't plan to). It's also very light and thin, adding to the portability. Nitpicks: The HDMI port is kind of in an awkward spot (at the end of the Hub rather than next to the USB ports) compared to other USB Hubs I've used; however, it's not a problem at all. Like all USB Hubs, it gets hot; however, it's not been a problem for me, even with all my devices plugged into it. Finally, the power draw issue. I've only had this happen to me twice, usually after changing the USB-C PD plug (right now a 67W charger, but I will upgrade to a 100W), but every time it would fix after unplugging and replugging everything back in, which is mildly annoying. If anything changes, I'll update my review.

reviews.title: Perfect Port Expander for M1 MacBook Air & M4 Mac Mini – Frees Up Ports Without the Hassle
reviews.body: I own a 2020 MacBook Air M1 (16GB RAM, 256GB storage) for mobile work and a 2024 Mac mini M4 (16GB RAM, 256GB storage) for my home office, and port limitations were driving me nuts, especially on the Air with just two USB-C ports. The UGREEN Revodok 105 5-in-1 hub, snagged for around $25, has been a lifesaver for expanding connectivity while keeping things simple and affordable. It’s plug-and-play on macOS Sequoia for both machines, and it perfectly hits my needs: charging, external displays, and legacy USB-A devices without dongle chaos. Here’s my experience after a week of heavy use. Pros: On the MacBook Air, this hub is a port-freeing champ. It uses one USB-C port and lets me charge via its 100W power delivery port with my 30W Apple adapter, leaving the second USB-C free for a Thunderbolt drive. I connected a 4K Dell monitor via HDMI (3840x2160 at 30Hz, sharp and stable), a USB-A keyboard, and an external HDD to the USB-A 3.0 port, which transferred a 50GB video project in under 5 minutes. No lag or disconnects. On the Mac mini, with its three USB-C and two USB-A ports, the hub adds flexibility. I plugged it into a front USB-C for a second 4K monitor via HDMI, using the native HDMI for my main display, and it handles dual displays like a dream. The USB-A ports ran my old USB stick and printer without issues. The aluminum build feels sturdy, stays cool even with all ports active, and is compact enough to toss in my bag with the Air. Battery life on the Air stays strong at 15+ hours. For the price, it’s a steal compared to Apple’s pricey adapters. Cons: The HDMI is 4K at 30Hz, great for work or editing but not ideal for gaming needing 60Hz—look at Thunderbolt hubs if that’s you. The two USB-A 2.0 ports are slow (480Mbps), so use the 3.0 port for fast drives. No SD card or Ethernet, but I didn’t need those. It warms up slightly under heavy load (charging, HDMI, data), but never hot. Tip: For the Air, connect hub, PD charger, then HDMI for a clean setup; pair a Bluetooth mouse to avoid USB-A clutter. On the Mini, use System Settings to extend displays for dual-monitor productivity. This hub is a must for Apple Silicon users needing more ports on a budget. It’s reliable, sleek, and does exactly what I need. Highly recommend!

reviews.title: Great USB C hub, can also serve as a dock
reviews.body: I bought this to use with a Minisforum mini PC I have to expand one of the rear type C USB 4 ports, not only for more connectivity, but to prevent regular plugging and unplugging from the computer itself. It's a great little hub with all of the IO I need, including an HDMI port which, honestly, I don't really need since the PC itself has both an HDMI and a DisplayPort connection. It provides 2 USB type A ports, two 10 Gbps type C ports and a third type C port that is capable of 100 watt power delivery. That combined with the HDMI output means this hub could also feasibly be used as a dock for something like a Steam Deck, ROG Ally, a laptop PC, etc. I tested it with my Steam Deck OLED and it worked just fine and was able to output an HDR signal to my LG television while charging the Deck at full speed since the Deck's charger puts out way less than 100 watts. It feels reasonably sturdy, has a braided cable and even a faint little LED to let you know when it's actually plugged in. The cable could have been a little longer, though it's serviceable since it spends its time just sitting on a desk right beside the PC. When I tested it with my Steam Deck though, to test whether it could serve as a dock for that, it was short enough that the hub couldn't lay flat on the desk behind the Deck and was sort of suspended in the air by the tension in the cable, which would probably damage it over time, so if you want to use this as a dock for another device I would consider mounting it to the back of the device's stand or to the wall or something to keep it from just hanging from its own cable. I also think more companies should consider opting for the more open Displayport instead of the more proprietary HDMI. Not having to pay licensing fees to use HDMI could have brought the cost down a little bit. Overall though it's easy to use, turns my otherwise hard to reach rear facing USB 4 port into something more accessible and can even charge attached devices at up to 100 watts. I'm pretty happy with the purchase and will definitely consider UGreen for my needs in the future.

reviews.title: better than expected

The hub works on my Windows laptop, my MacBook Pro, my iPad, and even my phone without any problems. It's safe to say that I have not run into any compatibility issues while using the ports hub. The cord length is a bit short for my liking, although the cord itself seems extremely high quality and durable, although it does get a bit hot after long periods of use, but nothing too out of the ordinary. Another problem is that while using the HDMI port connected to an external display, the transfer speeds dip really low, although it's not that big of a surprise, seeing that the max speed of this thing is only 10Gbps anyways, but it would have been even better if it used all 40Gbps of my thunderbolt 4 speeds. Overall, if you really need a new ports hub, I would go for this one, because it's extremely compatible, and it seems to be able to go for years without a replacement.

reviews.title: Good hub, but BEWARE: Your laptop MUST support "DP Alt Mode" for HDMI to work!
reviews.body: I build computers and I'm pretty tech-savvy, but even I missed a critical detail before buying this: Not all USB-C ports carry video. This UGreen hub is a "passive" device, meaning its HDMI port will only work if your laptop natively supports DisplayPort Alt Mode or Thunderbolt. My laptop - bought last year - has a single "Data-Only" USB-C port. The hub handles USB data perfectly, but the HDMI port is completely dead because my laptop physically cannot send video data through that port. So, how do you know if your laptop will support HDMI through this thing? Before you buy it, check the symbol next to your laptop's USB-C port. If it has a lightning bolt or a stylized "D" logo, it *should* work. If it has a battery icon or no symbol it's probably data-only and this hub's HDMI port won't work for you. You need an active "DisplayLink" adapter instead (and those have other limitations and can be laggy). Long story short, check your hardware first to make sure this is supported if you want HDMI. It's three stars for me, because this should've been a huge flashing neon sign when I bought it instead of a complicated footnote buried in an image.

The price...it solved a problem with it being the only solution I could find and is one of the less costly parts of my entire setup as well leaving me more room for expansion. Start the computer back up and nothing. Once again, I shut everything down and swapped cords around this time starting in the ports I hadn't used. What were in the new ports worked, the one drive that was in one of the others didn't work. What's kind of odd is the third problem port. sometimes will work if I plug something in while with everything on, but it's not seen on a reboot. It's built well and is really the best solution I have found for my setup. I gave it 3 stars when as it is now, doesn't deserve any, but they are sending me a replacement. A fully working version of this, that works longer than one day and hopefully for a long period of time is definitely a 5 star buy. Hoping this was just a fluke. Once I get the replacement and if it performs as it should I will update this review to where it should be. If not, I will downgrade it to also where it should be.

reviews.title: A hub is not a dock. This is a very good USB-C hub
reviews.body: Does what a hub ought to do - which is to say, you can plug it into one USB-C port and it will make power and data connectivity available to four downstream USB-C devices. The big caveats are that the host cable is extremely short and the power made available to downstream devices is significantly reduced from what the host provides. It's still a five star device because these short cables are universally present on all USB-C hubs, and the power limitations are less severe than other similar products that I have tested. Most importantly, the data connectivity offered by this unit is excellent, and it's extremely portable, being barely larger than the connectors it contains. I would still very much prefer a version of this device with a USB-C female connector on the back instead of the permanently attached short cable but apparently there are valid technical reasons that USB-C hubs are not made in this way. Devices that offer more power and better cabling options are now classified as docks rather than hubs, they tend to be based on Thunderbolt rather than plain old USB-C, and some of these docks are quite excellent, but they are comparatively very expensive. This particular device is just a hub, it is very affordable compared to a dock, and it's as good as USB-C hubs get.

reviews.title: Compact Hub With Fast Reliable Performance
reviews.body: I am giving this USB C hub 4 stars because it is a well designed accessory that makes it much easier to connect multiple USB C devices without taking up much space. The compact size fits easily into a laptop bag, making it convenient for travel, work, or keeping at a desk. The four USB C ports are very useful for connecting accessories like external drives, webcams, audio devices, and other peripherals. File transfers have been fast and reliable, and I appreciate that each port supports high speed data transfer. The 100W pass through charging is another great feature because I can keep my laptop powered while still using the other ports without constantly swapping cables. I also like that it works with a variety of devices, including laptops, tablets, and desktops that support USB C. The build quality feels solid, and everything connects securely without feeling loose. The reason I am giving it 4 stars instead of 5 is that it is important to know this hub is focused on USB C connectivity only. If you also need USB A, HDMI, or SD card slots, you will likely need an additional adapter. Depending on your setup, that may limit its versatility. Overall, this is a dependable and portable USB C hub that delivers fast performance and convenient charging. If your devices primarily use USB C, it is an excellent solution for expanding connectivity while keeping your workspace simple and organized.

reviews.title: Compatibility
reviews.body: I wanted this hub because I'm starting to experiment with videography on my iPhone 15 Pro, and the specs for data speed support and ability to support pass-through charging and other peripherals including a high-speed external drive made it seem ideal. And I'm sure it does all those things beautifully, but what it doesn't do is support charging of my iPhone..... which is a bit of a deal-breaker, really. Looking back, I see that the description doesn't actually mention support for iPhone 15 Pro, but iPad Pro and Mac compatibility (and support for supposedly universal USB-C devices) clearly doesn't include the iPhone. Very happy to accept that the reason for that is Apple and their outright stupid insistence on control of everything, but it doesn't really help me..... I've often bought Belkin accessories and peripherals and it's a brand I trust, so my "Value for money" and "Charging power" scores relate only to my immediate experience and inability to charge my iPhone. UPDATE 3 APR 2024: I've left all my ignorant waffle above in place in case any other users find the difficulty I had - and judging by the numbers who can't get their iPad to charge, there are several of us. I did uprate my "star" rating as the problem isn't Belkin and not even Apple, for a change :-) After some digging I found reference to a recommended power supply delivery of 100W, so phoned Belkin UK Support - and got straight through! Very helpful bloke took the details, looked up the specs, and confirmed that the MINIMUM permissible power supply to the hub is 85W and the RECOMMENDED rating is 100W. Less than that, and the hub won't allow pass-through to protect other components against possible excess current. Unfortunate, but I guess I'll have to shell out for an adequate PSU. My high opinion of Belkin kit is even higher now having experienced their support function. Very good indeed.

reviews.title: Do you have an external drive that has a short cable?
reviews.body: I have a LITE-ON USB 2.0 External CD/DVD Writer Model eUAU108, manufactured in 2013, with an attached cable that is slightly less than 4 inches long. This model was an improvement over prior models, in that it requires only a single USB 2.0 connection, whereas previous models employed a Y-cable to enable connecting to 2 USB ports simultaneously for additional power. I have always felt that this drive was marginally capable of running on the 500 mA specification for USB 2.0 ports. I think this is the main reason for the ultra short cable - to minimize the voltage drop. The short cable worked OK when I was using the drive with a laptop, but attempting to use it with a computer attached to the back of my flat screen monitor is a major problem. The USB ports are about a foot above the desktop, making it necessary to support the drive in some manner. This has always been problematic. I tried using the only USB extension cable that I had, a cheap dollar store cable, and it did not work at all. My next thought was that I should purchase a higher quality, and obviously more expensive, USB cable, but I still had reservations. Would a longer cable, even of a higher quality, work? Why did LITE-ON force a short cable onto the consumer? They could have provided a USB port instead of an attached cable. I then thought of using a powered hub, which could solve the voltage/power issue, but I still wondered if there might be other signal quality issues that a longer cable might cause. I believe I was starting to overthink the matter at this point! I started looking at the market of powered hubs and discovered that there was quite a variety, from no-name cheapies to surprisingly expensive higher end units. It was easy to eliminate the no-name cheapies because there were brand names I was familiar with that were very affordable. Then I discovered that some of the hubs were rated at 10 Gbps! Gotta have that feature, right? Even though I don't have a single device faster than 5 Gbps, I justified this feature on the basis of future-proofing. I figured it would only be a matter of time before I had devices of that speed. Later on I discovered that all the USB ports on the computer attached to the back of my monitor are 10 Gbps capable – five are USB 3.2 Gen2 (10 Gbps) and one is USB4 (40 Gbps!) - additional justification for going with a 10 Gbps hub. As I looked at the 10 Gbps offerings I quickly discovered that many, if not most of them, were from RSHTECH/Rosonway. They have quite a variety of well designed, useful devices. So many options that I found it helpful to generate a table of features to more easily compare them. I finally decided to go with the RSH-H7C4 for the following reasons: • 10 Gbps on every port • both USB-A and USB-C ports • push button switch (vs. rocker type), with an indicator light, for each port • all ports support USB Battery Charging 1.2 protocol (BC1.2), delivering a maximum of 1.5A at 5V (7.5W) per port [standard USB ports limit current to 0.5A (USB 2.0) or 0.9A (USB 3.2)] • 36W (12V/3A) DC power adapter • detachable 3.3 foot USB-C host cable (when I need to connect to a USB-A host I use a cheap adapter I purchased at a dollar store; some of the Rosonway units include a dual-headed cable with both A and C plugs!) • two year warranty It's a beautifully designed unit with a solid, weighty feel to it. Rounded edges and a thin accent band of non-anodized aluminum around each end give this hub a modern, classy appearance. With the case being narrow and slightly rounded on the bottom, one might have concern about its stability against the pushing and pulling of the connected USB cables. While it might technically be more stable with a completely flat bottom, it is surprisingly stable as is due to its weight and mass. Not at all like some of the lighter weight plastic cased devices that I have. It would take a deliberate effort to tip it over; I don't think that will be an issue. I actually do tip it over to accommodate one of my situations: the cable on my DVD drive is so short that the drive cannot lay flat when the cable is inserted into the port on the hub from above. I have to lay the hub on its side (see video). The included USB cable is heavy gauge, very thick. With my limited experience in the world of USB cables I have made two observations: 1)there is a tremendous range of cost, quality, and capabilities among the many cables on the market; 2)an extra USB cable frequently comes in handy. It would make sense to me that RSHTECH would provide a suitably high-grade cable with their hub in order to support the 10 Gbps data rate and the BC1.2 current draw capability. The fact that the USB cable is detachable is a bonus! It can be used elsewhere. I could even change it into an extension cable by the use of a gender-changing adapter. The indicator lights are a beautiful blue, quite small, but tastefull in my opinion; apparently too small for some reviewers, but I have no complaint. I would rather have them understated than overstated. The first testing I did was to connect the aforementioned LITE-ON CD/DVD writer to the computer hanging on the back of my monitor using the RSH-H7C4 hub and its included USB cable. (When the LITE-ON drive is directly attached to this computer I never have problems because the power requirement of the LITE-ON drive is easily satisfied.) I briefly tried the hub in “bus-powered” mode (without the power supply attached). I was able to read files on the DVD writer with no problem. (This was just a brief, not comprehensive, test because my main concern was testing the more power intensive task of burning a disk.) The next testing was in “self-powered” mode (with the power supply attached). I successfully burned and verified an ISO image. I then disconnected the power supply and tried to burn the image again in bus-powered mode. The burning went without any error messages, but the verification process failed. Another attempt in bus-powered mode failed during the burning process. Returning to self-powered mode (with the power supply attached), I was again able to successfully burn and verify the ISO image. It appears that when the DVD writer is attached through the hub and cable, burning a disk requires additional power beyond what the computer port is supplying (in order to power the circuitry in the hub and to compensate for loss over the length of the three foot cable). USB Battery Charging 1.2 protocol (BC1.2) seems to do the job here. I am pleased with that! I have solved the short cable issue; I can now lay my DVD drive flat on the desk and have dependable operation. Additional testing with a much older computer, a Dell Inspiron Mini 1012 (vintage 2010), revealed an unexpected limitation: the DVD writer was unable to be recognized as a boot device by the Inspiron Mini when connected to it through the hub. As far as I can tell, this is a limitation of the older BIOS in the Inspiron. There is no way to make this system recognize an optical drive connected via a USB hub at boot up. After the system is booted the drive is able to be used with no problem. It is my understanding that the more modern BIOSes of today handle this situation in a more sophisticated manner and can detect hub-connected optical drives at bootup. I verified this by bootup tests on the computer attached to my monitor and on a modern netbook. Both of those systems were able to recognize the DVD writer at bootup with no problem when it was connected via the hub. The Dell Inspiron Mini 1012 has USB 2.0 ports that theoretically should supply enough power for the LITE-ON CD/DVD writer, but I have always felt that it was marginal. I would like to be able to supplement the power. The RSH-H7C4 is only a partial solution here. It can be used with the Inspiron for burning disks since that is a process that occurs after bootup, but in the case where I need to boot from this DVD writer I might have to first transfer the DVD image to a bootable USB thumb drive and use that instead. While not a comprehensive evaluation of the RSH-H7C4, my tests have assured me that some of my problems have been solved. I can comfortably lay the LITE-ON CD/DVD writer on the desk instead of trying to figure out how to suspend it a foot up in the air in order to attach it to the computer hanging behind my flat screen monitor. I can also use the hub for more dependable disk burning using my Inspiron Mini 1012. I am quite impressed with the RSH-H7C4 hub and RSHTECH/Rosonway. I've always been very excited by little “boxes” and devices that solve computer interconnection (and other) problems. The companies that come up with these solutions are frequently very clever. RSHTECH will now be one of the first companies I look to for such solutions. A brief look at their lineup shows devices such as: • USB switches (to share USB ports between two computers) • powered and unpowered USB hubs, some with card readers and HDMI ports • powered USB extension cables • unpowered USB extension cables with built-in signal booster chips • USB HDD/SSD enclosures • docking and cloning stations • 10 Gbps USB connected M.2 NVME/SATA SSD enclosures • 10 Gbps USB connected Magnetic M.2 NVME SSD enclosure with 100W PD RSHTECH puts an effort into including enough hard facts and specifications in their product descriptions to enable consumers to easily understand a device’s capabilities and limitations. This fact, and my favorable impression of the RSH-H7C4 hub, give me confidence to expect good performance and value with any of their products.

reviews.title: Great Hub, Great Value!
reviews.body: Review of Rosonway 7 Ports USB 3.2 Hub 36W I purchased the Rosonway 7 Ports USB 3.2 Hub 36W and tested it in two separate configurations. First with my Surface PC laptop operating Windows and second with my Mac Mini 4 operating Sequoia. The Hub, which is powered with a 36W(12V/3A) DC power adapter, comes with 7 Ports, 4 USB-C 3.2 ports and 3 USB-A 3.2 ports. It claims speeds up to 10Gbps on every port. The Hub is small and sturdy aluminum device with independent electronic switches on each port and a blue LED indicator to display power status. This enables power management over all connected devices. When I connected it to my Surface laptop PC it worked seamlessly. I was able to connect to my external mouse and keyboard, 4 thumb drives and an external backup drive. The computer recognized all the drives and could rapidly access the external backup even with all these peripherals attached and running, the hub did not get hot (only warm as would be expected). I then put the hub through an extremely tough challenge. I connected it to my Mac Mini 4 through one of the rear-facing thunderbolt/USB C ports. I then connected all my peripherals to the hub. I did not use any of the other available Mac Mini ports, only the Ronsonway Hub. I connected the following peripherals: external Kensington Trackball mouse, a Seagate Portable 4TB External Hard Drive, two thumb drives, external speakers, a Xencelabs Quick Keys, and a backup UPS device and a second hub (7-Port USB C Hub Splitter 10Gbps with 3 USB-3.2, 4 USB-3.0 Ports) – this hub was connected to a Logitech camera. All of the peripherals worked perfectly. I could open and read all the external drives (the Seagate and the 2 thumb drives) the webcam, mouse and Quick Keys all worked without problems. Even with all these peripherals including the second hub attached and running, the hub did not get hot (only warm as would be expected). I couldn’t be happier with the performance of this compact, but powerful, hub. I made a brief video if you want to see the hub and the attachments I made to the hub. One final thought, I believe this hub is a terrific economical option for expanding a laptop or desktop to accommodate an amazing array of peripherals. This hub demonstrates that a single USB C connection to a Thunderbolt 4 port on my Mac Mini, can simultaneously and seamlessly accommodate a wide array of desktop components.

Pros: - Has connections for both USB A and USB C adapters - 36 watts of power was enough for all my devices (phone, watch, AirPods, big camera, small camera) at one time - Provides data connectivity at the same time as powering devices - Compact shape and light weight saves room in limited travel luggage - Individual switches to selectively power outlets as need changes CONS: - Could not support high-powered external pass-through power adapter - Not enough power for a large laptop (although it does charge smaller laptops and tablets)

reviews.title: Solid powered USB hub that has performed in the time I have used it.
reviews.body: I have been in IT long enough to know that a USB hub is one of those products that sounds simple on paper but has a surprisingly wide range of quality in practice. I have also been burned enough times by bad ones to approach any new hub with a healthy dose of skepticism. So when I say that the Rosonway powered USB hub has genuinely impressed me, I want you to understand that it is coming from someone who does not hand out compliments to peripheral hardware easily. I have had this hub for 13 days now. That might not sound like a long time, but in the context of my daily IT work, I have put it through what I would consider a serious run of testing. This is not a hub that has been sitting on a desk powering a wireless mouse dongle and a phone charger. It has been put through a ringer of a minimum of 12-14 hours 5-6 days a week. And it was used every day. With a rotating cast of demanding devices that would expose any weakness in a lesser product. Why I Came Back to Rosonway This is actually my second Rosonway hub. My first one is still running, still reliable, and was purchased specifically because I had grown so frustrated with other brands that I needed something I could actually count on. Before finding Rosonway the first time, I dealt with pretty much every problem a USB hub can throw at you — and often all at once. Devices dropping connection randomly. Transfer speeds that had no business being as slow as they were, even on a nominally high-speed hub. Units that died within weeks of purchase. Build quality that felt like it might give out at any moment. When you work in IT, unreliable hardware is not just an annoyance — it is a productivity problem and, at times, a professional one. The last thing I need in the middle of a task is a hub that decides to drop a device or throttle my speeds without warning. After going through several different brands and experiencing those issues repeatedly, I finally landed on Rosonway. My first unit solved all of those problems and has kept solving them ever since. So when I needed more ports, the decision to go back to Rosonway was not really a decision at all. It was the obvious move based on earned trust. Sure you could go with more notorious brands, but the bang for my buck on this brand has been optimal. Daily Use in an IT Context My use case is not casual. I run this hub daily as part of an IT work setup that includes both a PC and a Mac, and I switch between the two regularly. Cross-platform reliability is something I specifically look for and specifically test, because a hub that works beautifully on Windows but causes headaches on macOS is only solving half my problem. This one works correctly on both. No configuration differences, no quirks on one platform that do not exist on the other. It simply works the same way on both machines, which is exactly what you want. The range of peripherals I have connected through this hub over the past 13 days is wide. I have been running a wired USB-C to 3.5mm DAC for my Corsair headset with microphone — and I want to flag this one specifically, because audio devices are often where cheaper hubs start to show their weaknesses. A DAC demands consistent, clean power delivery. Any instability shows up immediately as audio dropout, static, or microphone signal issues. This hub has delivered clean, uninterrupted audio and microphone performance every single time. Beyond that, I have put external hard drives, thumb drives, and an SSD dock through this hub. External drives and SSD docks are about the most demanding things you can connect to a USB hub from a power and bandwidth standpoint. Drives pulling sustained power while transferring data will expose any inadequacy in a hub's power management quickly. I have had no issues — transfers run at expected speeds, the SSD dock behaves as if it is connected directly to the machine, and nothing has dropped or stuttered. I have connected all of these devices in various combinations, not just one at a time. Running multiple demanding peripherals simultaneously is where a lot of hubs start to fall apart, and this one has handled every configuration I have thrown at it without complaint. No Drivers, No Nonsense One of the things I appreciated immediately was the plug-and-play experience. There were no extra drivers to hunt down and install. On both the PC and the Mac, I connected the hub and everything worked. That is the experience it should always be, but it is not always the experience you get — especially when you are working across two different operating systems. Anyone who has spent time troubleshooting driver issues for what should be a simple USB hub knows how much time that can waste. The fact that this product required none of that was noticed and appreciated from day one. The Physical Setup The cable length on this hub is one of the practical details that does not always get mentioned in reviews but genuinely matters in a real workspace. It is long enough to allow for flexible positioning without being so long that it becomes a cable management problem. I was able to position the hub where it actually needed to be on my desk rather than compromising based on where the cable could reach. Small thing, but it adds up. The hub is powered, which is worth emphasizing for anyone who has tried to run demanding devices off a bus-powered hub and wondered why things were not working right. Having dedicated power through the included adapter means each port has what it needs to perform, even with multiple devices pulling from it simultaneously. For the kind of peripherals I am running — drives, an SSD dock, a DAC — powered is not optional. It is required. This hub delivers that without any hesitation. Thirteen Days and Counting I want to be honest about what 13 days of heavy daily use tells you and what it does not. It does not give you years of long-term reliability data. What it does give you is a solid read on whether a product is going to perform under real working conditions without hand-holding. I have not been gentle with this hub, in terms of use. I have been plugging and unplugging devices frequently, running demanding transfers, switching between operating systems, and connecting combinations of peripherals that test the power distribution. In all of that, I have not encountered a single failure, dropout, connection issue, or performance problem. That tracks with my experience with my first Rosonway hub, which is still running well after a year and half. The consistency between the two units tells me something about how Rosonway approaches quality control. It is one thing for one product to perform well. It is another for two separate purchases, at different times, to both deliver the same reliable experience. Who This Hub Is For If you are running a setup with demanding peripherals — external drives, audio devices, docking solutions — and you need something that will perform reliably across PC and Mac without driver headaches or connection instability, this hub is worth serious consideration. If you have been through the frustrating cycle of buying cheaper hubs, dealing with the problems they inevitably bring, and then replacing them, I understand that cycle because I lived it for longer than I should have. The Rosonway powered USB hub is not the flashiest product in the world. It does not need to be. It has been dependable so far. It does exactly what it is supposed to do, every time, without requiring you to babysit it or troubleshoot it or work around its limitations. In the world of peripheral hardware, that kind of consistency is a huge bonus in my line of work. Two for two on Rosonway products. I will be back if I need more ports. I am satisfied with my purchase.

reviews.title: Quality & design issues surfaced during usage
reviews.body: August 2023 update: On the 3rd week, my 2nd unit started to blink two hard drive connections on and off with only 3 ports switched on. Therefore rating is reduced to 1 star from 2. Initially, my 2nd unit successfully wrote 350 Gb drive to drive across this hub without any buffering errors (buffering errors are what usually goes wrong in such tests). Speed was about 40 - 70 mb per second for nominally-sized files. However was unable to complete a chkdsk on a mounted drive without terminating in a unidentifiable error (again usually what happens with bad hubs). My first unit which was returned had a bad port #3 (counting from the end plugs) and was causing disk errors evident in the Windows event viewer, which actually were errors when chkdsk was used (you cannot always trust the event viewer drive errors as Windows presumes any drive is where you left it from your last Windows session, so if you move it, or it is new to the location on its USD bus, the event viewer will scream bloody murder until it learns the new location, where it will then proclaim the drive is healthy). There appears to be a design deficiency in the hub: on both units I tested, there was too much noise on the final port #10 to plug in a cam. The cam image was very noisy and unusable. Plugging in the cam at the first port works around this design problem. Apparently, there is inadequate noise containment within the hub body, and this can cause slower transfer rates for hard drives and bad images for cams. Given the wide variety of hubs and potential for hub problems, and quality variance of Asian-pacific manufacturers, I am going to keep this one. Be sure to check each port when you receive yours.

reviews.title: VIA Labs chipset - so far so good
reviews.body: So far so good. Will update review if anything changes - have audio interface and few devices plugged in, external hard drive, sd card reader - no issues. For anyone curious about the chipset used, it's VIA Labs: VIA Labs VID_2109 PID_0822 (USB 3.2 hub) Primary 3-port hub + 1 downstream port (USBC) VIA Labs VID_2109 PID_0822 (USB 3.2 hub) Secondary 4-port hub off that downstream port (USBA) VIA Labs VID_2109 PID_2822 (USB 2.1 companion hubs) This was the only information I couldn't find before purchase, and was exactly what I was looking for - previously purchased a Amazon Basics 7 port usb3.1 hub and kept on getting errors in device manager. Seems like they just daisy chained a bunch of crappy hubs together to make it 7 port, and was bottle necked for throughput.

reviews.title: Works as well as powered hubs for music production
reviews.body: Update June 4, 2025: From 1 star to four stars After my review below I tried two other powered USB hubs. One did not work for my purpose described below, and the other performed just like this one, that is, it worked OK as long as I used the hub for the audio interface and laptop power, though it still complained that the power was low. I have since been told that my Dell XPS will issue that complaint because it has proprietary delivery. In either case, the battery stays well charged. So, I was hasty in dismissing this USB hub. It works as well or better than the other hubs I've tried since. Original review: This USB hub might be great for things like keyboards and mice, but I needed it to work with music production. I need to connect an audio interface (USB-A), an iLok license dongle (USB-C), and music samples on an SSD (USB-C). Since my Dell XPS has only three USB-C connectors, one of which is for power, I do need a USB hub. After a few weeks of misery, I discovered that if the SSD of music samples was plugged into this hub, the whole system would crash when I was running any Digital Audio Workstation (DAW). (For some reason it did not crash if I were running the stand-alone player, but piano notes would cut out occasionally.) Moving the SSD to a connector on the PC meant that I had to run power through this hub to the PC. My PC complained that the power was so low that I might observe a performance hit, but it did run. To free up a port for power, I tried plugging the iLok dongle into this hub, but then the sound from the music samples would halt after a few minutes. Bottom line is, I don't really know why this hub won't work with my music setup, but it does not. There is little consensus on the web about which hubs work best for music. I'll try a powered hub.

reviews.title: Great 10gbps USB-C Hub, worked with Anker support through compat issues with PD4 iteration 1
reviews.body: Original Review (updates below): ----- The moment I noticed this thing on Amazon, I bought it and it literally just arrived. Finally, 4K60 over just USB-C with other ports (including making up to 10Gbps available to them) for a reasonable price. Unfortunately, the first two things I've done with it were both disappointing. I'll cut to the chase, the power delivery pass through isn't working with one of their own chargers. The first device I tried connecting this with is my Anker PD4 with one USB-C cable as the only thing plugged into it so I can test the truly up to 100W (-15 for its own power) claims. I've tried connecting it with Apple's 2m USB-C charge cable (100w capable) and an equivalent CableMatters cable that also supports 100W. When plugged directly into my laptop, both of these cables immediately start charging it and show up as 100W power sources. When this Anker hub is plugged in and either of them is connected to the power delivery port on the side of it, the laptop does not charge (laptop is a 16" Macbook Pro, I've tried multiple ports just for the heck of it). My second complaint is that when absolutely nothing is plugged into it, it becomes fairly warm to the touch. Why, when it's doing nothing, is it hot? I'm clearly not running data or even power through it so I have low hopes for it under load. The fact that it doesn't work in exactly the scenario they want it to most (a MacBook Pro with one of their own chargers) seems like a pretty big fail. I've got lots of USB-C things though so I thought I'd grab a couple and try those. Using an Apple 96W USB-C charger, the device does pass through power delivery properly. It shows up as providing 79W to the laptop (siphoning off 17W in this instance). I also have a 56W Aukey charger that splits power between a USB-A port and a USB-C port that can provide 45W of power delivery. When plugged into that charger it does appear to work as well and appears in macOS as a 30W power source. Maybe the problem is the Anker PD4? But it works fine providing power to the laptop directly. Would love to hear from Anker about these two products working together and what I should actually expect. Having it be unreliable for power delivery isn't great, but power and heat aside (it is getting a little bit warmer now that it's providing power from the Apple power adapter, but still definitely holdable), the hardware looks and feels good and the cable feels durable. Worth also noting that there's a white LED ring on the side of it that appears to be always on when it's plugged in. Don't know why it needs an LED. ----- Update, June 22, 2020: I've done some more testing and Anker has reached out to me to investigate what might be the issue. I can say that the hub works as I would expect from a quick test with my iPad Pro 11" with the above functioning chargers. It was able to pass through power with the 96W Apple Charger on the other end to both the iPad port as well as a Magic Keyboard port. The ethernet adapter showed up in iOS settings and an external drive was functional. When connected via the Magic Keyboard, which is a power only connection, as expected it provided only power. Still no power passthrough of any kind when connected to the PD4. ----- Update July 1, 2020: I've written back and forth with Anker and they've sent me a replacement hub. It also doesn't work with the PD4. I've tried multiple USB-C cables but they have also shipped a cable to test with it. For now I'm increasing the review from 2 to 3 stars because I am more and more suspicious about the PD4 and less about this hub. They claim that they have tested the setup I have separately without issue, and I've sent video showing the problems I've encountered, so the troubleshooting is ongoing. Have had a chance to use Ethernet on it without issue. Still need to try to test out its throughput when trying to use a 10Gbps USB-C enclosure and a 4K60 monitor at the same time (+ ethernet). More updates to come. ----- Update July 10, 2020: I've continued to talk with Anker support and they shipped me a replacement PD4. The one I had was labeled as "Iteration 1" on its barcode, the one I got back was labeled "Iteration 2". I tested it out and it works perfectly with this hub, passing through the correct amount of power to multiple Macbook Pros and fast charging an iPad Pro. Clearly the fault doesn't lie with this hub and is instead an issue with the first iteration PD4, so I'm updating my review accordingly. Working with Anker support was great. I've also been able to test USB-C throughput (without driving a display as well so far) and it properly utilizes 10Gbps. I've attached some extra images showing various devices connected to it (keyboard dongle, SD card, USB-C 10Gbps external SSD enclosure, USB sound card, ethernet).

reviews.title: Like It, but it required additional equipment to charge iPad Air 4
reviews.body: I am exploring ways to make my iPad behave like a laptop, and with this little device, I am on my way. One of my primary concerns is that sometimes I have to troubleshoot routers at other people's homes. So I tried it out on my home. I found that I had to install an app from the manufacturer to make it work, then I had to reboot the router. Then, I got an amazing interface that was not the same as the interface on my laptop. It told me that I need a firmware update, but at this point, I am more comfortable doing the update on my laptop. One quirk I don't understand is that I plugged the PD port into my power cube, and the iPad told me it wasn't charging. That isn't good. I might have to return it and shop for a different brand. The newer Apple devices are awfully picky as to where they get their power from. Update: I found the email for Anker customer support, sent an email, and they got right back to me. Here is what they said: "Please first know: Due to the power input limitations of mobile devices, this hub can not provide pass-through charging to tablets (including iPad Pro/Air) or phones when using the original wall charger that came with your mobile device. To support full-speed charging for iPad Pro/Air, use an adapter that supports at least 15V (45W)." I found that the 3 foot power cord that Apple sent me is nowhere near long enough for charging while using the dock, so I sent away for a 45W charger and a 10 foot USB-C to USB-C charging cable that was compatible with iPad. Please be aware that Apple has circuitry embedded in the cord and you cannot use just any cord. The equipment I got was this: Charger https://smile.amazon.com/gp/product/B083BRKMJQ/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_asin_title_o00_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1 Cord https://smile.amazon.com/gp/product/B07LF1FNRV/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_asin_title_o00_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1 Cords are not rated in either volts or watts, so I sent another email to Anker asking if a 3 amp cable would work, and they told me that it should. Pay attention to the amperage when purchasing a cable to go with a high wattage charger. The cord that I purchased also comes in a 15 foot length. If this rig works, I will also purchase the 15 foot cord. The reason being that sometimes I need to do stuff in other people's houses, and I cannot count on a nearby outlet. I will update when the new equipment comes. Update: I installed a 45W charger with a USB-C TO USB-C cable that was advertised for iPads, and now my iPad is charging through the PD port, so that problem is taken care of. I sold the iPad and bought a 2019 MacBook Pro. The MacBook Pro has four Type C USB ports only, no others. I use one of the ports on the Mac for charging and another for the hub. I use the Type 3 USB ports on the hub for my mouse and graphic tablet. I like wired mice, because they use a wire for power, are more reliable, and do not generate dead batteries to pollute the environment. I wish the hub had an additional Type 2 or 3 USB port. Maybe I will buy an additional adapter, because I can't find a hub that sports the extra ports. I looked for a mouse that would plug into a USB C port, but did not find one to my taste. I like wired keyboards for the same reason I like wired mice. At any rate, all these wires that will not plug directly into my computer makes kind of a clutter, as depicted in my photo. Not much I can do about it at this stage of the game, however.

reviews.title: Convenient, but gets hot!
reviews.body: Pros Allows multiple devices (ext drives, keyboard) and Ethernet and HMDI cables to be plugged into one USB computer port (also has two card slots, SD and microSD) All devices can be disconnected from the laptop by pulling out one cable Can be powered either from the laptop, or from an external supply (not included) When powered from an external supply can provide power to the laptop Cons Gets very hot! This hub occupies one USB-C port on my new laptop, yet allows me to plug in two external hard drives and a keyboard. Most importantly, I can also plug in an Ethernet cable, to avoid the hassles (and security issues) of WiFi and take full advantage of my high-speed Internet connection. (I don't use the other features) In addition, I can route the power to the laptop through the same USB connection, potentially saving yet another USB port (while my MacBook has a separate power port, I can still use the USB for power). When I want to take my laptop somewhere (which is, after all, the whole point of a laptop!), I only need to unplug one thing. (Although I do have to remember to eject the external drives or I get a nagging reminder from the OS). The device gets very hot: I've measured 42C/108F with an IR thermometer. There is a warning label on the bottom saying that it may reach 122F (50C).This is disappointing: I got this unit as a replacement for another, similar unit from a different manufacturer that burned out on a hot summer day. (No, no flames and smoke, it just stopped working!) I got a small fan to cool the other unit on hot days (my room gets to 27C/81F). Now I'm concerned the same may happen to the Anker. I'll keep the fan on in the summer, I guess. The unit works as expected; I have gotten downloads from the Internet at speeds exceeding 600MB/s (probably limited by my ISP).

The Ethernet connection is stable and fast, which has been perfect for work calls and large file transfers. I also love how compact and portable it is while still offering plenty of connectivity options. HDMI output looks great, USB ports transfer quickly, and the SD card reader is very convenient for photo and video work. Anker continues to deliver reliable products, and this hub is no exception. reviews.title: Almost perfect, could use one more USB-C Gen 2 port and a metal case instead of plastic.
reviews.body: Never really had any problems with Anker gear, I've come to trust the brand name. This little hub is almost perfect for use with my 2019 MacBook Pro, but where Anker really dropped the ball is by not adding one more USB-C port. I mean, there's two, but if one is dedicated to power devices only that doesn't really leave much room for expansion by only giving you one extra, I mean they were thoughtful enough to give you two USB-A ports. I do like that the USB-C and two USB-A ports are version 3.2 Gen 2 rated for up to 10Gbps transfer speeds versus Gen 1 at 5Gbps. The plastic casing does get hot, not sure if aluminum metal would be any better, but it would feel nicer, plastic just feels cheap. Also, a dark case with dark letter printing doesn't work because you can't see the writing, should have used lighter letter coloring. Otherwise, solid performer. I'll keep it along with my other one because having two hubs with a laptop is convenient so I don't have to always haul a hub around from place to place. PROS: • 1 USB-C port version 3.2 Gen 2 rated up to 10Gbps. • 2 USB-A ports version 3.2 Gen 2 rated up to 10Gbps. • Also includes, HDMI, Ethernet, SD and micro SD card ports. CONS: • Plastic casing, gets hot. • Should have one more USB-C port. • Port description lettering is too dark, gets lost against dark case color, should have used white or silver lettering instead. • No audio port.

reviews.title: Read this if you are having issues
reviews.body: I bought this a while back and while shopping for a second dock for my wife, I came across a lot of reviews where people are complaining about this thing. I relate to those experiences, but the problem is not the dock itself. Mine worked at first and then it started to work intermittently. Sometimes, my external monitor would come on and sometimes it wouldn't. I tried it with different Anker cables (I had been using the one that came with it) and I even tried it with different Macbooks. At one point, I actually thought the problem was probably with Apple. It was really frustrating and annoying. But then I decided to try a new Thunderbolt 4 cable I had purchased from Cable Matters. I didn't really expect that to make a difference, but it solved everything. It has worked perfectly for over a year now. I connect my laptop and I can instantly use my monitor and get to work without a hassle. I've since realized that while Anker makes good power bricks and even hubs, they make really crappy cables. I have a LOT of them, unfortunately. They short out very quickly and I've noticed they often separate near the connectors. For stuff like lightning cables, you know right away when it stops working. But Thunderbolt cables can be confusing because they don't just fail. A bad cable will work really well sometimes and then not at all other times. It doesn't make sense that you would get perfect resolution on your monitor one day and not even be able to get it to turn on the next. For high bandwidth like 4K external monitors, you really just need a high quality, reliable cable. Don't try to save money on that and don't buy cables from Anker. I hope this is helpful to people.

reviews.title: Six ports done right — everything works at full spec simultaneously
reviews.body: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Six ports done right — everything works at full spec simultaneously Been through enough USB-C hubs to know that the spec sheet and the real world performance are two different conversations. Hubs that claim 4K HDMI but throttle to 1080p under load, or PD charging that slows to a trickle the moment you plug in a display — these are the failure modes that make hub shopping frustrating. The UGREEN Revodok delivers on every spec simultaneously without compromise. 4K HDMI output is clean and stable — no signal dropout, no resolution negotiation on reconnect, just a solid 4K signal from the moment the hub is plugged in. Color accuracy and refresh rate are correct without any manual display configuration needed. Drives a 4K monitor without any of the flickering or handshake issues that plague cheaper hubs. 100W PD charging passthrough is the other critical spec and it holds up under real load. Laptop charges at full speed while simultaneously driving the HDMI output and pushing data through the USB ports — no thermal throttling, no charge speed reduction from splitting duties. The hub handles the power budget correctly which is not a given at this price point. Gigabit Ethernet is a legitimate gigabit connection — ran a speed test to confirm throughput matches a direct connection without the bottleneck that USB-C Ethernet adapters sometimes introduce. Stable link with no dropped packets under sustained transfer load. Build quality is classic UGREEN — aluminum housing, tight port tolerances, USB-C connection to the host that seats firmly without wobble. Compact enough for travel without sacrificing the port selection that makes it useful at the desk. Six ports, full spec, no compromises. Highly recommended.

reviews.title: An effective low-cost expander
reviews.body: I have a relatively new Mac Mini M4, and I do find its ports somewhat limiting. The Mac has two USB-C in front and three Thunderbolt ports in the back. Because the Mac mini itself is so small and light, it can be difficult to access the ports and plug peripherals in and out. This UGreen USB hub works connected either to the USB ports in the front or to one of the Thunderbolt ports in the back. It doesn’t offer Thunderbolt speed, but it is quite quick and responsive for USB-C. I have had minor reliability problems with the ports on the M4—I have a USB keyboard, trackball, backup drive, and sometimes two external SSD drives plugged in, and the Mac itself sometimes doesn’t see everything at the same time—for instance, my trackball sometime disappears. I’ve had this hub plugged into one of the USB-C ports in front and keep a number of peripherals plugged into it, and they have all worked very effectively at the same time, and the speed has been very responsive on the external data drives. So it has improved my Mac. This is not heavy; it’s light plastic, but it works well. What I would have appreciated is if this had one USB-A port, too. I see a lot of USB-A hubs that have one C and a lot of As, but the new standard is USB-C. Some of my peripherals are USB-A, and I have little adapters that convert USB-A to USB-C and those work great with this, too, so with one of those, you can, of course, plug USB-A items into this. This has been very helpful to me with my M4 Mini and I recommend it.

reviews.title: The Travel Dock in My Laptop Bag
reviews.body: What I like Plug-and-play. One USB-C cable in, several ports out. No drivers, no setup, no configuration. HDMI output for plugging into a hotel-room TV or conference projector without an adapter. SD card reader for moving photos off a camera. The microSD reader is a bonus. Two USB-A ports are enough for a mouse, a USB stick, or a card reader I already own. 85 W pass-through charging means I can keep my laptop charged through the hub when I have a USB-C charger handy. Lives in the laptop bag and is ready when I travel. It is the kind of accessory that pays for itself the first time you really need it. Compact and light. I forget it is in the bag until I need it. What annoys me Not a daily driver on my home desk. My home computers already have the ports I need, so the hub sits in the bag most of the time. Bus-powered. No battery, no separate power input. I am not trying to power a hungry external device through it, so this is fine, but it is not a “real docking station” with its own power supply. One HDMI output. If I wanted to drive two external monitors, I would need a different hub or a dock with display-multiplication support. The transcript says “second HDMI port,” and this hub gives me one, not two. No Ethernet port. Wireless works almost everywhere I travel, but a wired Ethernet jack would be a real bonus on hotel networks that block Wi-Fi or charge for it. I do not actually use it on my Mac mini. It would work, but I have not built the habit of plugging the mini through the hub. That is a me problem, not an Anker problem. Who it is for, and who should skip it If you travel with a laptop and need HDMI, an SD card reader, extra USB-A, and the option to charge the laptop through a single cable, this is the right tool. It is small enough to leave in the bag and useful enough to justify its weight. Skip it if you want a full desktop dock with its own power supply, multiple display outputs, Ethernet, and the ability to drive a multi-monitor workstation. That is a different product class, and a single USB-C hub with bus power will not do that job. Skip it if your laptop already has every port you need. The hub is solving a missing-port problem, and if you do not have one, it will just sit in your bag. Verdict The Anker USB-C 7-in-1 hub is a small, useful travel accessory that lives in my laptop bag and earns its place every time I take a trip. It is not exciting. It is not a daily driver. It is the kind of thing that disappears into your workflow and then you are grateful for it when you need it. Grade: A—if you want a single-cable travel dock for a laptop or Mac mini. Buy the linked listing if your use case matches mine.
